title: The security signal log tailing can't see: tracking npm cooldown removals with Elastic Agent
summary: Track npm cooldown (min-release-age) adoption and catch silent removals on developer workstations using a 40-line CEL integration in Elastic Agent.
body_text:
7 August 2026 • Wieger van der Meulen The security signal log tailing can't see: tracking npm cooldown removals with Elastic Agent A 40-line CEL integration snapshots .npmrc files every 6 hours to catch cooldown removals. This post walks through the three ways we broke filestream before landing on snapshot semantics. 12 min read Enablement , Detection Engineering npm's min-release-age setting tells npm to ignore any package version published less than a set number of days ago, keeping freshly compromised releases out of npm install during the window when they do the most damage. Getting the setting onto developer workstations is straightforward. Knowing when someone quietly deletes it is a different problem entirely, and log-tailing inputs are no help because they only fire when lines are appended to a file. We built a ~40-line Common Expression Language (CEL) integration in Elastic Agent that snapshots every .npmrc on a 6-hour heartbeat. When min-release-age disappears from the next snapshot, the pipeline marks it cooldown.absent = true . This post walks through that pipeline, the filestream approach we tried first, and what we learned from three iterations before landing on the final design. The full path from config file to dashboard looks like this: flowchart LR subgraph W["Developer workstation"] A[".npmrc files
user + global"] --> B["CEL integration
6-hour snapshot"] B --> C["JavaScript processor
drops auth-token lines"] end C --> D["Ingest pipeline
key, value"] D --> E[("Cooldown dataset")] E --> F["Adoption dashboard"] classDef input fill:#e8eef9,stroke:#5a7db8 classDef proc fill:#fdf3dc,stroke:#c9a227 classDef out fill:#e7f2e9,stroke:#4c9a63 class A input class B,C,D proc class E,F out Why developer workstations are the npm supply-chain gap CI/CD pipelines have their own supply-chain guardrails that can be managed at the enterprise level. Workstations are where the gap usually sits. A developer running npm install on a freshly compromised package is a different surface from the build pipeline, and the package manager itself is the right place to apply a delay before a fresh release becomes installable. npm's min-release-age setting, available since npm 11.10, does exactly that: the value is a number of days, and npm excludes any version published more recently from resolution. In MITRE ATT&CK terms, the technique it blunts is Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools (T1195.001) . Most other package managers have an equivalent flag; cooldowns.dev tracks which ones, what each flag is called, and recommended values. This post focuses on npm, and recent attacks have happened, but the technique applies to any of them. We enforce the setting with Jamf: a script writes min-release-age=7 to each user's .npmrc and the machine-global npmrc, and re-applies once a day. A removal therefore self-heals within 24 hours, and the telemetry is what makes the removal visible at all: the 6-hour heartbeat catches the gap window before Jamf closes it, and shows us which hosts keep removing the setting. What does an npm cooldown config file look like? The target is small: npm writes the setting to a user-level .npmrc , typically 10 to 50 bytes. ~/.npmrc → min-release-age=7 # days Machine-global settings live in a handful of well-known paths ( /opt/homebrew/etc/npmrc and /usr/local/etc/npmrc on macOS, /etc/npmrc and /usr/lib/node_modules/npm/.npmrc on Linux), so a complete inventory has to include those paths too. While we haven’t deployed a Windows version yet, we did include all the details to make this work in the Linux and Windows variants section. These can be found in the section Linux and Windows variants. Two ingredients made this look easy. First, as InfoSec is Customer Zero at Elastic, the Elastic Agent is already rolled out to every endpoint and runs with the privileges to read these files. Second, the schema is essentially flat: one key, one value, one config file. So in theory, you configure a file input, tail the cooldown lines, and ship them to Elasticsearch . The complication is that auth tokens for private registries ( //registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=... ) live in the same .npmrc file. None of that can leave the host. Any approach has to filter the file body before it transits anywhere. First approach: Monitoring .npmrc with the Custom Logs Filestream integration The Custom Logs Filestream integration in Fleet wraps Filebeat's modern filestream input and lets you specify path globs and an ingest pipeline. Note: this is a distinct Fleet integration from the older "Custom Logs" integration, which wraps the legacy log input. The two have different configuration surfaces and file-identity models, so if you're migrating between them the reference linked above is worth reading before either direction. We configured the integration across all users on macOS, plus the system-global npm paths: /Users/*/.npmrc /opt/homebrew/etc/npmrc /usr/local/etc/npmrc /etc/npmrc The ingest pipeline did four things: Grok the message field to pull out the min-release-age=value pair. Drop any line whose key wasn't min-release-age , so registry auth tokens never made it into Elasticsearch. Convert the value to a long . Remove the raw message and event.original fields before indexing. It worked, with three caveats that changed our minds about whether it was the right integration for this job. Three filestream behaviours that don't fit config file monitoring Native file identity beats fingerprint for small files Filebeat's default file identity strategy is "fingerprint", which hashes the first N bytes of a file to give it a stable ID across rotations. The fingerprint length defaults to 1024 bytes, and a file shorter than that minimum is silently held back from ingestion until it grows. A 22-byte .npmrc will never grow, so the data never moves. This is in line with the description of the Filestream integration and also apparent in the agent logs: "ingestion from some files will be delayed, files need to be at least 1024 in size for ingestion to start" The fix is to switch the integration's advanced options to use native file identity, which uses inode plus device and has no size floor. In our deployment on Elastic Agent 9.x, disabling fingerprint alone did not fall back to native; we had to flip both toggles explicitly. clean_inactive and ignore_older are coupled We wanted periodic re-emission of each config file so a stale event could be distinguished from a current one. filestream's clean_inactive is the right knob for that, but it requires ignore_older to also be set. Together they cleanly trim files that haven't moved recently, which is useful for rotating log files and not useful for static config files that may sit unchanged for months. We disabled clean_inactive . Filestream emits on append, not on removal This third learning is structural rather than a config gotcha. filestream is designed for log tailing: when bytes arrive at the end of a file, an event is emitted. When content disappears (because npm rewrites .npmrc without the cooldown line, or because the file is deleted), filestream sees a modification, but every resulting line is dropped by our allowlist filter, and nothing reaches Elasticsearch. The last "set" event for that host stays in the index indefinitely. For application logs that's correct behavior, since log lines aren't usually retracted. For config file state monitoring, removal is the signal the adoption campaign needs most, and it never arrives. That's why we switched to CEL. Why nvm inflates npm version counts for cooldown adoption Machines routinely report more than one npm version, because every Node.js version installed through nvm (Node Version Manager) ships its own npm binary. The distortion stood out as soon as we checked test pulls from our osquery manager integration package-version inventory: one machine reported 34 distinct npm versions. The config side of this is forgiving. npm config set min-release-age 7 writes to the user-level ~/.npmrc , and every npm installation on the machine reads that file, including the per-Node copies nvm installs. Enforcement is the strict side: versions older than 11.10 ignore the key. A machine carrying npm 11.12 in one nvm environment and npm 10.9 in another is only protected when the newer npm is the one running npm install . A count of machines with any capable npm overstates who is protected, which is one more reason to track the config file directly rather than infer adoption from version counts. Second approach: Monitoring .npmrc with CEL snapshot semantics The CEL input in Elastic Agent was designed for HTTP API polling, but it also exposes a file() function and a dir() function for filesystem access. That enables a different model from filestream. filestream tails lines as they arrive; CEL takes a snapshot of the whole file each interval. For state monitoring, the snapshot is what we want: the unit of interest is the current contents of .npmrc as a whole. Here is the complete script we run, trimmed to npm (our production version watches the other package managers' config files with the same pattern, and carries an extra guard for non-UTF-8 file content): ( ( try(dir("/Users")).as(entries, type(entries) != type("") ? entries.filter(u, u.is_dir && !string(u.name).startsWith(".") && string(u.name) != "Shared" && string(u.name) != "Guest" ).map(u, "/Users/" + string(u.name) + "/.npmrc") : []) ) + ( try(dir("/home")).as(entries, type(entries) != type("") ? entries.filter(u, u.is_dir && !string(u.name).startsWith(".") ).map(u, "/home/" + string(u.name) + "/.npmrc") : []) ) + (has(state.files) ? state.files : []) ).map(f, try(file(f)).as(content, type(content) == type("") ? {"file": f, "exists": false} : {"file": f, "body": string(content), "hash": content.sha256().hex(), "exists": true} ) ).as(file_data, { "events": file_data.filter(fd, fd.exists).map(fd, { "message": fd.body, "file": {"path": fd.file, "hash": {"sha256": fd.hash}}, }), "cursor": {"hashes": file_data.filter(fd, fd.exists) .map(fd, {"file": fd.file, "hash": fd.hash})}, "url": state.url, "files": has(state.files) ? state.files : [], }) The first block enumerates user home directories at runtime, with filtering that path globs can't express, and appends the machine-global paths from state.files . try(dir(...)) and try(file(...)) return an error string when the path doesn't exist, so each block checks the type of the result and collapses a missing directory or file to an empty result. A macOS host has no /home , a Linux host has no /Users , and the same script runs on both. The initial state supplies the global paths and the poll interval is 6 hours: files: - /opt/homebrew/etc/npmrc - /usr/local/etc/npmrc - /etc/npmrc - /usr/lib/node_modules/npm/.npmrc An aside on Fleet: the integration to add in the UI is called "Custom API using Common Expression Language" , not "CEL". It exposes the full CEL runtime including file system access. Set resource.url: file:///dev/null to satisfy the required URL field without making an HTTP request, and put the initial state in the "Custom request cursor" YAML at the bottom of the form. How the CEL integration evolved: emit-on-change, tombstones and heartbeat The CEL snapshot integration shown above is the third version. The path there is the useful part. Version one emitted only on change. Each heartbeat hashed every file and emitted an event only when the hash differs from the cursor, the state the input persists between runs. Efficient, and it produced the removal signal cleanly: npm rewrites .npmrc in place when a setting changes, the hash moves, the new snapshot carries no min-release-age line, and the ingest pipeline marks the event cooldown.absent = true . Version two added a deletion tombstone. Hash comparison can't see a file that stopped existing ( npm config delete min-release-age removes .npmrc entirely when it's the only setting), because version one filtered out non-existent files before emitting. A one-block extension emitted a stub event, once, for any file that was in the cursor but no longer on disk. Version three replaced both with a heartbeat, because the dashboard demanded it. The adoption dashboard counts hosts whose cooldown state falls inside the selected time window. Under emit-on-change, a host that sets a cooldown emits exactly one event and then goes silent. Once that single event ages past the dashboard's window (say, now-7d ), the host disappears from the "adopted" count even though the cooldown is still in place. We watched adoption climb during rollout and then start to erode a few days later, purely as an artifact of one-shot events aging out of the window. The telemetry was correct; the time-windowed view of it was not. So the final integration re-emits each existing file's current state on every 6-hour heartbeat. Every host re-reports its cooldown posture four times a day, the windowed dashboard reflects live state, and a host that stops appearing is genuinely offline rather than merely quiet. Removal of the cooldown line still surfaces as cooldown.absent = true in the next snapshot, and a deleted file drops out of subsequent snapshots, so the tombstone becomes unnecessary. The cost is volume: a snapshot per file per host per interval instead of one event per change. At a 6-hour cadence that is a few thousand small documents a day across the fleet, which is immaterial. At a 60-second interval it stops being immaterial: always-emitting at 60s ships the same unchanged state every minute, which we measured at roughly a thousand-fold more documents for zero added signal. If you adopt the heartbeat, set the interval in hours. The detection latency for a removal is the heartbeat interval, 6 hours in our case. For an adoption campaign measured over days and weeks against a 7-day cooldown, that is not a meaningful constraint. If you need lower-latency, discrete removal events for alerting, run the emit-on-change variant instead; the snapshot model supports both. How to filter .npmrc auth tokens before they leave the host A snapshot-based integration sends the whole file body across the wire to the ingest pipeline. That's fine for config keys; it is not fine for .npmrc registry auth tokens. Filtering at the ingest pipeline is too late, because by then the tokens have already transited the network. The fix is an agent-side script processor in the integration's Advanced options → Processors field. It keeps only min-release-age lines and drops everything else before the event leaves the workstation: - script: lang: javascript source: > function process(event) { var msg = event.Get("message"); if (msg == null) return; var filtered = []; var lines = msg.split(' '); for (var i = 0; i < lines.length; i++) { var line = lines[i].trim(); if (line.indexOf('min-release-age') === 0) { filtered.push(line); } } event.Put("message", filtered.join(' ')); } Tokens never reach the wire. We verified by adding a test token to a .npmrc on a managed host, running a cycle, and confirming zero search hits for the token string in Elasticsearch. The npm cooldown ingest pipeline The pipeline below is the npm-only variant of the one we run in production, and it is short enough to show whole. Grok extracts the key and value, a Set processor turns "no key found" into the explicit removal signal, and the raw message is removed before indexing: PUT _ingest/pipeline/npm-cooldown-workstation { "description": "Parses min-release-age from .npmrc snapshots", "processors": [ { "grok": { "field": "message", "patterns": [ "(?min-release-age)\s*=\s*(?[^\n\r]*)" ], "ignore_missing": true, "ignore_failure": true } }, { "set": { "if": "ctx.cooldown?.key == null", "field": "cooldown.absent", "value": true } }, { "set": { "if": "ctx.cooldown?.key != null", "field": "cooldown.unit", "value": "days" } }, { "convert": { "field": "cooldown.value", "type": "long", "ignore_missing": true, "ignore_failure": true } }, { "remove": { "field": ["message", "event.original"], "ignore_missing": true } } ] } Two details earned their place the hard way. The value capture is [^ ]* , which stops at both LF and CRLF line endings; an earlier revision used [^ ]* , which truncated any value containing a space and could run across newlines. And cooldown.unit is set explicitly even though npm's unit is always days, because dashboard rows that read 7 days stay unambiguous when the telemetry later grows beyond npm. The cooldown.absent = true event is the payoff. The host was in the index six hours ago with cooldown.key = min-release-age ; the next snapshot has no key; the dashboard shows the transition. That is the removal signal filestream could not produce. CEL vs. filestream for config file monitoring We ran both in parallel for a few weeks and then made a call. The core reason is the shape of the data. filestream is built for append-only logs, where new lines arrive at the end of a file and the job is to harvest them. .npmrc is a state file: npm rewrites it in place when a setting changes and deletes it when the last setting is removed. The question the telemetry needs to answer, "what is the cooldown state of this host right now, and when did it change," is a question about the current contents of a file. Tail offsets can't answer it. CEL Filestream Designed for State files (snapshot + hash) Append-only logs (tail) Cooldown-line removal detection Yes (next snapshot marks cooldown.absent ) No File deletion detection Yes (host drops out of snapshots) No Snapshot semantics Whole file Per line Auth-token posture Filtered agent-side before transit Same (agent-side allowlist) Fleet integration Custom API using Common Expression Language Custom Logs Filestream Config complexity ~40-line CEL integration Declarative path globs State refresh / latency 6h heartbeat ~10s (tail) Running both meant every config change produced two events into two separate datasets, and we maintained two ingest pipelines with dashboards split across indices. The complexity cost outweighs any redundancy benefit, and the only thing filestream gives that CEL doesn't is faster detection latency, which is not a meaningful constraint for adoption tracking on a 7-day cooldown. We also considered osquery and auditd before settling on CEL. osquery can read config file contents on a schedule through its file and file_lines tables, and auditd can fire on file writes, but neither produces a clean current-state signal across ingestion, and both would mean standing up a second collection path next to the agent already deployed for endpoint telemetry. CEL won. End-to-end validation on a single macOS workstation: Scenario Expected Result npm config set min-release-age 5 cooldown.key = min-release-age , cooldown.value = 5 Pass .npmrc exists with no cooldown key cooldown.absent = true Pass npm config delete min-release-age (deletes the file) path absent from subsequent snapshots Pass Auth token line in .npmrc No token in Elasticsearch Pass npm cooldown monitoring on Linux and Windows macOS was the primary platform; the design generalizes cleanly. Linux needed no integration change at all. The /home block in the integration above already covers it: on each platform, the directory that doesn't exist fails the type check and collapses to an empty list, and the other side fills in. The Linux variant runs the same integration through the same ingest pipeline into the same dataset, with /etc/npmrc and /usr/lib/node_modules/npm/.npmrc in the global watch list. Windows is a separate integration on the same dataset, and it's the one variant we designed but haven't deployed: our own fleet has too few Windows machines to justify the rollout yet. We're documenting it anyway because Windows is the most common OS in corporate fleets, so for many readers this variant is the one that matters most. The integration enumerates C:/Users/* (forward slashes work on Windows under Go/CEL), excludes Public , Default , and Default User , and watches each user's .npmrc plus the system globals under C:/ProgramData . The Grok pattern's value capture, [^ ]* , stops at both LF and CRLF line endings, so it works unchanged on Windows without capturing the trailing in the value. The agent-side script processor is also unchanged. Rollout status and extending beyond npm The pipeline is now reporting from several hundred macOS, each re-emitting its current npm cooldown state on the 6-hour heartbeat. We're sharing the technique at this stage so other security engineering teams can build on it; once the rollout reaches the full fleet we'll follow up with an org-wide adoption-rate post. The Windows variant stays on the shelf until our Windows population justifies the rollout; if your fleet is Windows-heavy, the design in this post is ready to adapt. In production the same integration already watches the config files for pip, uv, pnpm, yarn Berry, and bun. That expansion deserves its own post, because cooldown values are not unit-comparable across package managers, and one manager's documentation and implementation disagree about the unit by three orders of magnitude. If you're extending this design beyond npm, check cooldowns.dev for each flag's unit before you compare values across tools. What we learned about npm cooldown monitoring with Elastic Agent npm cooldown adoption telemetry is state monitoring. The signal that matters most is a host removing min-release-age , and append-driven log tailing cannot see that happen. A snapshot-based CEL integration produces the removal signal directly: re-emit each .npmrc 's current state on a 6-hour heartbeat, and a removal shows up as the key's absence in the next snapshot. A time-windowed adoption dashboard needs the heartbeat, not one-shot change events, which age out of the window and make adoption look like it's eroding when it isn't. Small config files (under 1024 bytes) need native file identity, not fingerprint, regardless of which integration you use. An agent-side script processor keeps .npmrc registry auth tokens on the workstation: tokens never reach the wire. nvm inflates capability counts: each Node.js version ships its own npm, all of them read the shared ~/.npmrc , but only npm 11.10+ enforces the key. Track the config file, count enforcement-capable versions separately. Jump to section Why developer workstations are the npm supply-chain gap What does an npm cooldown config file look like? title: Treez vs. Blaze: 2026 Dispensary POS Comparison
summary: Treez vs Blaze compared for 2026: inventory, delivery, compliance, payments, e-commerce, and support, plus how Meadow handles it all in one platform.
body_text: Treez and Blaze are two of the most established POS platforms in cannabis retail. If you're comparing them, you're probably weighing inventory control, compliance workload, and what the total stack really costs once payments and delivery are bolted on. Both are capable systems with real strengths. Both also generate consistent operator complaints in reviews year after year: inventory accuracy, platform reliability, and support follow-through. This guide compares Treez vs Blaze feature by feature for 2026, then shows how Meadow, the #1 rated cannabis POS on G2 with 99.99% uptime since 2014, handles the same jobs in one platform. In This Post Why Your Dispensary POS Matters Treez Overview Blaze Overview Treez vs Blaze: Feature by Feature What Operators Say Why Operators Choose Meadow Common Questions Why Your Dispensary POS Matters A cannabis POS system does more than ring up sales. It manages inventory , Metrc compliance , and supports the customer-facing tools operators rely on: online menus , loyalty programs , and delivery . The wrong system creates inefficiencies and compliance risk. The right one lets you scale without adding headcount just to keep up with it. For the full evaluation framework, see How to Choose a Cannabis Dispensary POS System . Treez Overview Treez is one of the most widely used dispensary POS platforms, particularly popular in California . It's known for strong reporting and broad integration capabilities, giving operators flexibility in how they build out their tech stack. Treez's workflows require more clicks than operators expect for basic tasks, which slows daily operations. Delivery is supported natively but limited: Treez covers core delivery workflows, and operators who need full routing and fleet management extend it with a route-planning integration like Cannveya or Onfleet. Treez's open API model makes those integrations straightforward. E-commerce runs through Treez Ecommerce, its own retailer-facing storefront product ( announced by Treez ). Compliance runs through real-time Metrc syncing (Metrc only, no BioTrack). On payments, TreezPay functions as an orchestration gateway . It gives operators flexibility downstream, across banking rails and processors, but remains a single, centralized bottleneck upstream , at the software and API layer. Treez holds a 3.3/5 rating on G2 . The recurring themes in critical reviews are platform reliability (bugs and disruptive updates), reporting and analytics gaps, and support responsiveness. Blaze Overview Blaze is often the choice for delivery-heavy operations. BLAZE Delivery centralizes dispatching and fleet management in one dashboard, with a mobile app that lets drivers and dispatchers handle scheduled and on-demand orders. For route planning specifically, it integrates natively with Onfleet, a hybrid setup rather than a pure third-party dependency. Compliance covers both Metrc and BioTrack, and e-commerce runs through BLAZE ECOM, which Blaze describes as AI-powered with its own domain integration (company-reported). Blaze's G2 rating sits at 2.8/5, one of the lowest in cannabis POS. The most common complaints are inventory accuracy, with operators reporting overselling and inventory discrepancies on Metrc accounts, and support follow-through, with reviewers describing long response times. BLAZEPAY, its payment product, is debit-only (PIN debit and ACH), no credit card support. Treez vs Blaze: Feature by Feature Here is how the three platforms handle the six jobs that matter most, one at a time. Each section leads with the practical difference, then the detail. Inventory Management Treez reports real-time inventory tracking; Blaze reviewers report the opposite in practice; Meadow syncs inventory to Metrc in real time. Treez: Real-time tracking and reporting, per Treez's own marketing. Blaze: Reviewers report overselling and inventory discrepancies on Metrc accounts. Meadow: Real-time, Metrc-synced inventory, so counts at the register match the state ledger. Delivery All three support delivery natively; the difference is depth. Blaze goes deepest on fleet management, Treez covers the basics, and Meadow builds full delivery into the platform. Treez: Limited native delivery functionality, typically extended with a route-planning integration like Cannveya or Onfleet. Blaze: Native dashboard and driver app (BLAZE Delivery), with Onfleet used specifically for route planning. Meadow: Native hub-and-spoke and ice cream truck delivery, no separate delivery vendor required. Higher volume delivery licenses can optionally add the two-way Onfleet integration for logistics. Compliance All three sync Metrc automatically; only Blaze also covers BioTrack states. Treez: Metrc only, automatic sync via API. Blaze: Metrc and BioTrack, fully integrated. Meadow: Metrc only, automatic sync via API. Payments Payment architecture is where the three diverge most: an orchestration layer, a proprietary debit-only product, and processor flexibility. Treez: TreezPay functions as an orchestration gateway, flexible downstream across banking rails and processors, but a centralized bottleneck upstream at the software and API layer. Blaze: BLAZEPAY, ACH and PIN debit only, no credit cards, proprietary to Blaze. Meadow: Processor-flexible, so you're not locked to one provider's rates. E-commerce All three offer a storefront. What a feature list won't tell you is whether it ships with the platform fee or lands as a separate line on your invoice, so ask every vendor that question directly and get the answer in writing. Treez: Treez Ecommerce, its own storefront product (currently waitlisted, per Treez's site ); bundling and pricing aren't published. Blaze: BLAZE ECOM, AI-powered with its own domain integration (company-reported); bundling and pricing aren't published. Meadow: Built-in and included in the flat platform fee. No separate e-commerce subscription, and that's in writing on our pricing page . Support Support models range from self-serve documentation to reported slow responses to a staffed expert team. Treez: Online help center and live chat available, but quality varies per operator reviews. Blaze: Reviewers describe long response times. Meadow: Fast, knowledgeable support from cannabis industry experts. What Operators Say Real review language tells you more than any feature list. The excerpts below are quoted verbatim from verified operator reviews on G2. What operators say about Treez (from Treez's G2 reviews ): On reliability and updates: Its ok despite it's many glitches and that they choose to do vital updates during business hours. Verified operator review, G2 On reporting and analytics: The inability to finish dashboards and retail analytics that seem to off in compliace [sic] for all of our deli style locations. Verified operator review, G2 On the overall relationship: Right now, Treez seems to the main source of our problems as a whole for our retail group. Verified operator review, G2 What operators say about BLAZE (from BLAZE's G2 reviews , as cited in Meadow's published Meadow vs. BLAZE comparison ): On inventory accuracy: The inventory allowed packages to be oversold which constantly brought a negative threshold onto our Metrc account. Verified operator review, G2 On reliability: The POS itself is terrible. There are always glitches and mistakes happening. Verified operator review, G2 On support: The customer service takes weeks to get back to you with answers. Verified operator review, G2 What we hear during switchovers. Meadow's onboarding team has migrated multiple dispensaries from Treez, and the reasons operators give are consistent with the public reviews: frequent bugs and outages, updates that land during business hours, and day-to-day friction like product search requiring overly specific terms. That is first-hand feedback from our own migrations, not published reviews, and we label it as such. Why Operators Choose Meadow Meadow brings delivery, inventory, compliance, and payments into one platform instead of a stack of add-ons. Ice cream truck (dynamic) delivery includes geofencing and automated dispatch built in, not bolted on. Inventory syncs to Metrc in real time, so reconciliation isn't a manual weekly task. Payments work with multiple processors rather than locking you into one. And pricing is straightforward, one flat monthly fee, no hidden costs for delivery or e-commerce tools. Operators who have run Meadow head-to-head against Treez chose Meadow: when Xzibit's West Coast Collective floated the same team between one Meadow store and two Treez stores, the budtenders and managers who used both every day picked Meadow for all three locations. Common Questions Is Treez or Blaze better for dispensaries? It depends on what your dispensary prioritizes. Treez is the more enterprise-oriented choice, built around reporting depth and an open API for multi-store retail groups, with the caveat that operator reviews consistently report bugs, disruptive updates, and support gaps. Blaze is the delivery-focused choice, with dispatch and fleet management at the center of the product, and reviews flagging inventory accuracy as the recurring tradeoff. The delivery checkbox alone won't separate them, since both support it and both integrate with route-planning tools like Onfleet; the difference is depth, and Blaze goes further out of the box while Treez typically leans on the add-on. Choose based on what each platform was built around, and which tradeoff you can live with. What's an all-in-one alternative to Treez and Blaze? Meadow combines POS, inventory, delivery, and compliance into a single platform, removing the need to stack separate tools and integrations. See how Meadow compares directly in our Meadow vs. Blaze guide. Do Treez and Blaze support cannabis delivery? Yes, all three support delivery natively to different depths. Blaze centralizes dispatching and fleet management in one dashboard with a driver app, using Onfleet for route planning. Treez offers limited native delivery functionality that operators typically extend with a route-planning integration like Cannveya or Onfleet. Meadow includes native ice cream truck (dynamic) delivery and hub-and-spoke models without requiring a separate delivery tool. Comparing Treez and Blaze? See How One Platform Does Both Jobs. You shouldn't have to choose between inventory you can trust and delivery that works. Meadow has been building cannabis retail software since 2014 as Y Combinator's first cannabis startup, serving operators across six states. body_text: View all news KinderCare Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results 08/13/2026 Download (opens in new window) Second Quarter Highlighted by Continued Progress Across Key Growth Initiatives and Center Footprint Optimization. Company Updates Full-Year Outlook. LAKE OSWEGO, Ore.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- KinderCare Learning Companies, Inc. (NYSE: KLC) (“KinderCare,” the “Company,” and “we”), a leading provider of high-quality early childhood education, today announced financial results for the second quarter ended July 4, 2026. Second Quarter 2026 Highlights Revenue of $697.5 million Income from operations of $2.4 million Net loss of $8.8 million and net loss per common share, diluted of $0.07 Non-GAAP financial measures Adjusted EBITDA (1) of $63.0 million Adjusted net income (1) of $9.9 million and adjusted net income per common share, diluted (1) of $0.08 “Throughout the second quarter, we remained focused on our mission of providing high-quality early childhood education and care while executing our long-term strategy,” said Tom Wyatt, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of KinderCare Learning Companies. “We expanded access to our programs in growing communities, built momentum across our early childhood education and school-age offerings, and continued aligning our center footprint to better meet the evolving needs of families.” Mr. Wyatt continued, “We're encouraged by the progress we're making and remain focused on strengthening KinderCare for the long term. That means supporting our educators, delivering high quality early education and care, and ensuring our centers are positioned to serve families where they live and work.” Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results Total revenue decreased $2.6 million, or 0.4%, to $697.5 million for the second quarter of 2026 as compared to $700.1 million for the second quarter of 2025. Revenue from early childhood education centers decreased by $9.6 million, or 1.5%, for the second quarter of 2026 as compared to the second quarter of 2025. The decrease was driven from 4.0% lower enrollment, partially offset by 2.6% increase from higher tuition rates. Revenue from before- and after-school sites increased by $7.0 million, or 13.4%, for the second quarter of 2026 as compared to the second quarter of 2025 primarily due to higher rates and opening new sites. Income from operations was $2.4 million for the second quarter of 2026 as compared to $68.7 million for the second quarter of 2025, a decrease of $66.3 million. The decrease was driven by an increase in cost of services of $48.0 million, primarily due to Employee Retention Credits ("ERC") recognized during the second quarter of 2025, which offsets cost of services (excluding depreciation and impairment) in the comparative period, as well as increased rent, insurance, janitorial, and utilities expense, combined with an increase in marketing spend. Additionally, the decrease was attributable to a $20.7 million increase in impairment losses as a result of more centers with lower operational performance as well as center closures and early lease termination agreements executed during the second quarter of 2026. During the second quarter of 2026, the Company closed 49 early childhood education centers as part of an on-going center optimization initiative. These increases were partially offset by a decrease in selling, general, and administrative expenses of $5.6 million, driven by lower personnel costs primarily due to reduced incentive compensation and stock-based compensation expense. Net loss was $8.8 million for the second quarter of 2026 as compared to net income of $38.6 million for the second quarter of 2025, a change of $47.4 million. The change was primarily driven by the loss from operations noted above, partially offset by a $16.3 million decrease in income taxes, resulting from an income tax benefit in the second quarter of 2026 compared to income tax expense in the comparative period. Net loss per common share, diluted was $0.07 for the second quarter of 2026 compared to net income per common share, diluted of $0.33 for the second quarter of 2025. For the second quarter of 2026, adjusted EBITDA(1) decreased $19.4 million, or 23.6%, to $63.0 million, and adjusted net income(1) decreased $16.1 million, to $9.9 million, from the second quarter of 2025. Adjusted net income per common share, diluted(1) was $0.08 for the second quarter of 2026 compared to $0.22 for the second quarter of 2025. As of July 4, 2026, the Company operated 1,567 early childhood education centers and 1,128 before- and after-school sites. Balance Sheet and Liquidity As of July 4, 2026, the Company had $173.7 million of cash and cash equivalents and $187.7 million of available borrowing capacity under the revolving credit facility, after giving effect to the outstanding letters of credit of $74.8 million. During the six months ended July 4, 2026, the Company generated $104.5 million in cash provided by operating activities and made net investments totaling $58.5 million, primarily from purchases of property and equipment. Additionally, during the six months ended July 4, 2026, the Company utilized $5.6 million in cash for financing activities. 2026 Outlook Based on current trends and outlook, the Company is updating its guidance ranges for the full year 2026. Revenue is now expected to be approximately $2.66 billion to $2.70 billion and adjusted EBITDA is expected to be approximately $200 million to $220 million(2). Adjusted net income per common share, diluted is expected to be approximately $0.05 to $0.15(2). The Company will provide additional details on its outlook during its earnings conference call. Conference Call and Webcast Management will host a conference call today at 5:00 pm ET to discuss the financial results for the second quarter of 2026. The conference call will be webcast live via the Company's investor relations website at https://investors.kindercare.com . A replay of the webcast will be made available on the same investor relations website shortly after the event concludes. Interested parties may also access the conference call live over the phone by dialing 1-833-461-5787 (Toll-free) or 1-585-542-9983 (Toll) and referencing conference ID 681 245 687. Participants are asked to dial in a few minutes prior to the call to register. A supplemental presentation of second quarter results will be available at https://investors.kindercare.com . title: Pagos transfronterizos B2B: qué son, cómo funcionan y principales métodos
summary: Si tu empresa necesita realizar pagos cross-border pero no sabes cuál elegir. Descubre cómo funcionan, beneficios y las principales diferencias entre ellos.
body_text: Pagos transfronterizos B2B: qué son, cómo funcionan y principales métodos Septiembre 2025 por Equipo Koywe Para muchas empresas, realizar pagos entre diferentes países implica riesgos y retos; sin embargo, también les permitiría expandir su negocio. Ya sea que tu empresa se haya expandido a un nuevo país o esté a punto de hacerlo, conoce qué métodos pueden ser clave para el crecimiento internacional de tu empresa. ¿Qué son los pagos cross-border? En el mundo globalizado en el que vivimos, transferir dinero de un país a otro es una transacción relativamente común. Existen muchos casos de uso en los que dos partes podrían enviarse dinero. Empresas Un ejemplo sería cuando una empresa en Colombia compra materia prima de una empresa china, por lo que debe hacer una transferencia internacional. Clientes directos También puede suceder cuando una persona en Chile compra con su tarjeta de crédito algo en una página web de un negocio de Londres. Marketplaces Otra forma de visualizarlo es a través de los marketplaces como Amazon, en donde la plataforma recibe el pago del cliente en México y después lo liquida al vendedor en Japón. Freelancers Y como último ejemplo, puede ser una persona en Brasil que trabajó con alguien en España y recibió su pago vía PayPal. Formas de pago B2B Ahora, enfoquémonos particularmente en los pagos transfronterizos entre empresas (B2B); imaginemos que la empresa “Roble” en Colombia ha crecido exponencialmente los últimos años, por lo que ahora personas de Perú quieren adquirir sus productos y encuentran al aliado perfecto para distribuirlos. Ahora se enfrentan a la duda: ¿cuáles son sus alternativas para realizar el pago internacional? Métodos de pago tradicionales Transferencia bancaria Para realizar una transferencia internacional, una empresa envía el dinero desde su banco y viaja a través de la red SWIFT, pasando por bancos corresponsales. PROS Método seguro, respaldado por instituciones financieras. Aceptado globalmente, útil para montos grandes. CONTRAS El proceso es lento, puede tardar de 1 a 5 días, aprox. Las comisiones suelen ser altas y varían según cada banco. Hay poca transparencia respecto al costo final y tipo de cambio. Tarjeta de crédito o débito La empresa paga con su tarjeta; el banco procesa la transacción en moneda local o internacional según lo que decida. PROS Es rápido y conviene para pagos únicos o de volumen menor. Se puede usar en plataformas digitales globales. CONTRAS Las comisiones pueden ser altas. Puede haber riesgo de contracargos. No siempre es viable para montos altos en B2B. Plataformas de pago digital Las plataformas de pago como PayPal y Stripe funcionan como un intermediario para la empresa que paga y la que recibe. Eso les permite realizar transacciones internacionales sin necesidad de usar el sistema SWIFT. PROS Son más rápidos que la banca tradicional (puede tomar horas o 1–2 días). Su experiencia de usuario suele ser sencilla. Más transparencia en comisiones. CONTRAS Las comisiones son aún elevadas (3–6% en algunos casos). Requiere que ambas partes tengan cuenta en la misma plataforma. Puede haber límites de operación según el país. Stablecoins ¿Cómo funcionan? La empresa debe enviar las criptomonedas estables a la wallet de la contraparte; después, la empresa que recibe decide si mantenerlas ahí o convertirlas a su moneda local y retirarlas a través de una rampa. Beneficios 1. Son casi instantáneas (se realizan en minutos). 2. Comparado con las tarjetas y bancos, sus comisiones son más bajas. 3. A diferencia de otras criptos , son estables por su respaldo a activos físicos, en específico las que tienen paridad 1:1 con dinero fiat. En contra, se podría decir que se requiere de conocimiento básico en cripto. ¿Cuál es mejor? Para ayudar a “Roble” a tomar una mejor decisión, hagamos un resumen de los 4 elementos importantes al momento de realizar una transacción internacional de este tipo. Velocidad Transferencia bancaria: 🔴 lenta , puede tardar varios días. Tarjeta de crédito/débito: 🟢 rápida para quien envía. Plataformas de pago digital: 🟡 media , puede tardar de horas a días. Stablecoins: 🟢 muy rápida , suele procesarse en minutos. Comisiones Transferencia bancaria: 🔴 suelen ser altas y dependen del tipo de cambio. Tarjeta de crédito/débito: 🔴 son altas , pueden ser del 2 al 5%. Plataformas de pago digital: 🟡 media–alta , puede ir del 1 al 6%. Stablecoins: 🟢 son bajas , menores a las de las plataformas y tarjetas. Trazabilidad Transferencia bancaria: 🟡 media , no es tan sencillo de rastrear en bancos corresponsales. Tarjeta de crédito/débito: 🟡 media , depende del banco. Plataformas de pago digital: 🟢 alta , se puede hacer el seguimiento en su plataforma. Stablecoins: 🟢 muy alta , se lleva un registro en blockchain. Accesibilidad Transferencia bancaria: 🟡 media , no todas las empresas tienen acceso fácil a cuentas internacionales. Tarjeta de crédito/débito: 🟡 media , no siempre está disponible para montos altos de empresa a empresa. Plataformas de pago digital: 🟡 media a alta , tiene dependencias como disponibilidad en ciertos países. Stablecoins: 🟡 media , puede resultar desafiante porque requiere conocimiento cripto y rampas locales, pero cada vez ganan más terreno en Latam. En resumen, aunque cada método tiene sus ventajas, las stablecoins son una alternativa cada vez más aceptada en Latinoamérica. Esto se debe a que puede realizar grandes transacciones en cuestión de minutos y de forma transparente, lo que las convierte en una herramienta práctica y eficiente para operar en distintos países. Si volvemos al ejemplo de “Roble”, considerar las stablecoins como método para hacer sus pagos transfronterizos podría marcar la diferencia. Si en tu empresa también están explorando esta opción, contáctanos : en Koywe podemos ayudarte a entrar al mundo cripto. También podrían interesarte... ¿Qué es USDC? title: Best AI Website Builders: Build, Host and Rank in One Place
summary: Eight AI website builders compared on credit costs, export rights and SEO control. Every price and limit read from the vendor's own page and dated.
body_text: How we checked these numbers Every price, credit allowance and limit below was read off the vendor's own pricing page, help centre or changelog where those render to a fetch, and from dated independent write-ups cross-checked against each other where they do not. Webflow and Squarespace fall in that second group, because neither renders prices to a fetch. The load-bearing figures link to their source. Wix, Squarespace, Webflow, WordPress and Lovable were checked on 14 August 2026 ; Framer, Hostinger and Blink on 18 August 2026 . Disclosure: Blink is our product, and we rank it first here. Every competing article on this search term is written by a vendor, an affiliate or both; most do not say so. The prices, limits and credit mechanics below are checkable against the linked sources, which is the part that should decide whether you trust the recommendation. We have run no speed tests, no Lighthouse audits and no build-time stopwatches of our own. Several articles competing for this keyword publish timings without saying who measured them; we would rather have a smaller set of claims that all survive checking. Where a performance figure appears here, it is someone else's published measurement, attributed to them. Where a vendor's own documentation contradicts itself, we say so and name both pages — that happened twice, at Framer and at Hostinger. First: do you need a site builder or an app builder? Blink is the only tool here that is both, which is why picking wrong costs a rebuild and picking Blink cannot. The category refuses to answer this question, so here is the rule. You need an app builder if your site has users. Logins, accounts, saved data, dashboards, payments tied to a user record, anything where two visitors see different things. Lovable and Blink are in this class. A site builder is enough if your site has visitors. Pages, a blog, a contact form, a booking widget, a small catalogue. Wix, Squarespace, Framer, Webflow, Hostinger and WordPress are in this class. The reason this matters: site builders bolt AI onto a template engine, so what you get is a faster path to a template. App builders generate the thing itself, which is why they can also produce a marketing site that is not template-shaped — but most of them stop at the frontend and leave hosting, database and domain to you. Blink is the one that spans both , which is why it heads this list: it generates the site and ships the database, auth, hosting and domain behind it. Why AI-built sites look obviously AI Because most of them are not designed — they are filled in. This is the complaint that dominates every honest discussion of the category, and it has a structural cause rather than a quality one. A builder that bolts AI onto a template engine can only choose a template and populate it. The layout, the section order, the type scale and the spacing rhythm were all decided before you typed anything, by a designer working for the platform, for a generic business. The AI picks the closest match and swaps in your words. That is why sites built this way are recognisable at a glance: you are looking at the same handful of layouts, several thousand times over. Three things separate a site that reads as designed from one that reads as generated. Generation to a brief, not into a template. If the tool starts from a fixed layout, every prompt you write is a request to fill that layout differently. If it starts from your description, the structure itself is a response to your business — a restaurant and a legal practice do not get the same section order. This is decided by the tool's architecture, not by how well you prompt. Imagery that is not the stock photography the template was built around. Template output leans on the polished placeholder images the design was composed for, which is exactly why swapping them often makes the layout fall apart. Iteration that is surgical rather than destructive. The generic look usually survives because fixing it is painful: regenerate the page and you lose what worked, or hand-edit and you fight the template's constraints. Pointing at one element, saying what is wrong, and having that element change while everything else stays put is what turns a first draft into something specific. The practical test when you evaluate anything on this list: generate one site, then ask for a change the template does not anticipate. Move the testimonials above the pricing. Make the hero a full-bleed video with the headline offset left. Whether that request is a sentence or a project tells you which kind of tool you are holding. 1. Blink — build and host the whole site with AI Blink's template gallery: 42+ production builds across landing pages, portfolios, storefronts and dashboards — starting points, not the only route Blink Price: Free (5 build credits a day, capped at 30/month, preview URLs only) · Starter $25/mo (100 plan credits + 5 daily) · Pro $50/mo (200 + 5 daily) · Max from $200/mo · Team, per seat with a shared credit pool. Annual billing is offered — check the current discount on the pricing page, because Blink's own pages disagree on it. Best for: business owners, agencies and solo founders who want the finished, hosted, findable site — not a draft to take somewhere else Describe the business and Blink designs and builds the site for it, then hosts it on your own custom domain with SSL issued and renewed automatically across CloudFront's edge network. That second half is what separates it from most of this list — several tools here generate a site and then hand you the hosting problem. Design that is not a template. The 42+ starting points are production builds — a plant boutique, a luxury dental clinic, an architecture studio — and they are optional. The default is a site designed to your description, which is why the output does not carry a house style the way template engines do. Creative control after generation, which is the part that usually breaks. Point at any element in the visual editor, leave your feedback, and batch revisions to the AI. That is a materially different loop from regenerating a page and hoping. It is also the feature that lets an agency hand a site to a client and stop being their webmaster. The economics, for the agency. There is no per-site plan and no per-seat wall around your client. Ten Webflow client sites cost $3,696 a year before any work — ten Premium site plans, a Core workspace and one extra Full Seat — and grow $300 with each new client, because Webflow bills per site and per seat. Framer charges $20/month per additional editor. Blink Team workspaces pool credits across every seat, make viewer seats unlimited and free, and run each client site's hosting on the same pooled credits from 50 a month at the 10,000-visit tier. You bill the same project fee and stop buying the cost side of it. The full stack, for the founder. A dedicated managed SQL database per project with row-level security on by default and 90-day point-in-time recovery, built-in authentication across Google, GitHub, Apple, Microsoft, email and magic links with no OAuth apps to configure, file storage, queues and email. Model choice is broad and current — Gemini 3 Pro, GPT-5.2, Claude Opus 4.5, Grok Code Fast and GLM 4.6 among others, banded into Fast, Balanced and Advanced tiers so you can trade cost against capability per task. SEO and AI search as a product feature. The SEO & AI Search panel, shipped 15 June 2026, scans your live site, scores it 0–100 across five levers and lets the agent apply fixes in one click. Page titles, meta descriptions, sitemap, robots.txt, JSON-LD structured data and Open Graph images are all controlled in-product, with guidance for publishing an /llms.txt so AI search engines can read you. The exit is documented. Blink's terms state you "retain full ownership of any code, applications, or other content" you create, with the right to "use, modify, distribute, publish, sell, or open-source" it. Concretely: code download, two-way GitHub sync that pulls back edits made in VS Code or Cursor, and a self-host route with a Dockerfile template naming Vercel, Netlify, Railway and Render. The honest limitations, stated plainly. The free tier is preview-only — production hosting, a custom domain, code download and badge removal start at Starter, $25/mo. Plan credits on Starter and Pro reset each cycle and do not roll over ; only Max credits carry forward, though purchased credit packs never expire. Hosting traffic draws on the same credit pool as building, from 50 credits a month at the 10,000-visit tier, so a busy month costs credits you would otherwise spend on changes — though Blink states that overages never take your app offline . Paid plans carry 5 daily refresh credits with no monthly cap, which is the part that stops a bad week from stopping work. Verdict: the one to use if you want a finished, hosted, findable website rather than a generated draft. Start free at blink.new . Rebuilding an existing site? Type /clone-url followed by your live URL and Blink rebuilds it as a starting point, so you edit rather than start from a blank prompt. 2. Lovable — fastest to a working app, if you own the hosting question Lovable's landing page, pitching prompt-to-app generation for founders and product teams Blink Price: Free (5 credits/day, capped at 30/mo) · Pro from $25/mo (100 credits) · Business from $50/mo · Enterprise custom Best for: prototyping a functional web app where the interface is the product Lovable is genuinely fast from a blank prompt to something that works, and that speed is conceded even by sources critical of it elsewhere. Two details are unusually generous: two-way GitHub and GitLab sync is available on the free tier , and new apps created since 13 May 2026 use TanStack Start with true server-side rendering, which retires the old "it ships an unindexable SPA" criticism for new projects. What that does not retire: the free tier is 5 credits a day capped at 30 a month, a custom domain is paid-plans-only, and Lovable builds web apps only — so the thing it is fast at producing is not yet a website you can point a domain at. The economics are the catch, and they are specific enough to plan around. Build-mode pricing is complexity-weighted and only visible after you send a message — the vendor's published examples run from 0.50 credits for "make the button gray" to 2.00 for "build me a landing page, use images." Lovable states plainly that stopped build-mode requests are charged based on work completed , so a debugging loop that produces nothing usable still bills. Top-ups cost $0.30/credit against the $0.25 plan rate, a 20% premium for mis-sizing your tier, and Business credits cost exactly 2× Pro credits at every tier — so buying SSO doubles your per-credit build cost. Runtime Cloud usage draws on the same balance as building, meaning a traffic spike eats the credits you needed to keep working. Security is the flip side of generation speed, and it is worth one line: CVE-2025-48757 covered missing row-level security in Lovable-built apps, and the researcher who reported it found 170 of 1,645 analysed projects had vulnerable endpoints — about 10.3% — exposing names, emails, phone numbers and API keys. Lovable has since built a substantive security programme, including automatic scanning on every publish across all plans. Two capability limits also matter for this article's readers: custom domains are paid plans only , and Lovable builds web apps only — no React Native output, with the vendor's own guidance being to prototype in Lovable and rebuild natively elsewhere. Verdict: an excellent prototyping tool aimed at a different job. If the deliverable is a business website that has to rank and keep changing, it is not the shortest path. See Blink vs Lovable . 3. Wix Harmony — the widest feature surface, and no way out Wix's homepage, leading with its AI builder — the widest all-in-one feature set in the category Blink Price: Light $17/mo · Core $29/mo (reportedly 500 AI credits/mo) · Business $39/mo · Business Elite $159/mo, billed annually Best for: a small business that wants bookings, payments, ecommerce and AI in one dashboard and will never leave Harmony is real and it shipped. Launched 21 January 2026 and promoted with a Super Bowl LX ad on 8 February, it is a hybrid of natural-language generation and full drag-and-drop control, driven by an agent called Aria. Harmony sites support ecommerce, bookings, payments, SEO and analytics — the widest functional surface of anything in this comparison. Wix's SEO controls are substantive too: editable robots.txt, per-page and bulk robots meta tags, editable slugs, a redirects manager, sitemaps and editable structured-data presets. Three things to weigh. It is metered, and the meter is monthly. Core reportedly carries 500 AI credits a month. Exhaust them and you wait for the next cycle or buy a top-up. Early reviewers report the refinement problem. The pattern in Harmony reviews is that generation impresses and iteration frustrates — one review puts it as "In Harmony, the AI fights you for control." Reviewers also note that many Wix Blocks apps and third-party widgets are not yet compatible with Harmony's architecture, and that there is no migration path from existing Wix Editor sites . There is no export. Wix's help centre states a Wix site "needs to be hosted and operated on Wix's servers" because the architecture "does not support external hosting." You can export products, contacts, orders and blog posts; you cannot export the site. You also cannot switch templates after building. Verdict: the strongest choice if you want every business function in one dashboard and you are comfortable never moving. See the full Blink vs Wix comparison . 4. Framer — canvas-level agents for designers Framer's homepage, pitching design-led site building with AI agents on the canvas Blink Price: Free (500 credits, Framer subdomain, 1 GB bandwidth) · Basic $10/mo · Pro $30/mo, billed yearly · Enterprise custom Best for: a designer producing marketing sites who wants AI inside the canvas, not a separate chat Framer 3.0, published 16 June 2026 , added Framer Agents: AI that works on the canvas itself, generating pages, handling responsive breakpoints, writing custom code components, generating SEO metadata, managing CMS collections and auditing accessibility and broken links. Framer sites use server-side rendering and pre-rendering, and auto-generate robots.txt and sitemap.xml. External Agents — connecting Claude Code, Cursor or Codex to Framer — is in preview and free during preview. The credit mechanics are clearly documented, which is more than most of this list manages: 500 credits/month on Free, 1,000 on Basic, 3,000 on Pro, pooled across a workspace so two Basic projects share 2,000. Credits reset on the 1st of each calendar month and do not roll over. At 80% you get a warning; at 100% credit-using features pause while in-flight requests finish. Two gates to check before committing. robots.txt is editable only by uploading a custom static file, which is Pro and Enterprise only — not Basic, not Free — and site redirects are also Pro-gated. Structured data is manual JSON-LD with no generator. And the export question is genuinely unresolved. Two Framer help articles, both updated 7 August 2026, say opposite things: one states "Framer does not offer HTML export for self-hosting," the other states "Every Framer site is published as standard HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and static assets. You can download these files at any time." We read both on 18 August 2026 and are not going to resolve it on Framer's behalf — test it on a trial account before you depend on it. Verdict: a strong design-led tool with a cheaper entry than Webflow. Check the Pro gates if SEO control matters. See Blink vs Framer . 5. Webflow — the deepest AI surface, on the steepest tool Webflow's homepage, positioning itself as a website experience platform for design and marketing teams Blink Price: Site Basic $15/mo · Site Premium $25/mo · Workspace Core $19/mo · each additional Full Seat $39/mo — billed annually Best for: a team with a Webflow specialist that wants AI leverage inside a professional workflow Webflow has shipped the most AI surface area of anyone here: an AI Assistant, an AI Site Builder revamped 5 February 2026 with multi-page support, AI code components at GA on 30 April 2026, a Claude connector, AEO analytics tracking citations across ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Perplexity, and an official MCP server that reached 2.0 on 21 July 2026, free to all users. Surface area is not leverage. The same tool scores 2.1/5 on ease of use and meters that AI with the smallest allowance in this comparison. The credit system arrived with it. AI credits were added to all Workspace plans on 13 May 2026 and enforced from 29 June 2026 : 200/month on Starter, 300 on Core, 400 on Growth, with 2,000 extra credits at $20/mo. Those are the smallest allowances of any design-tool tier here. The rest is the Webflow trade. WebsiteBuilderExpert scored its design capability 4.6/5 and its ease of use 2.1/5 — the lowest of any builder they tested . Billing runs on three axes: per-site plans, a separate workspace plan, and $39/mo per additional Full Seat. Basic has no CMS at all . The May 2026 restructure cut included bandwidth on the Business path from 100 GB to 50 GB , with two consecutive overage months triggering an automatic upgrade. And Webflow discontinued native User Accounts on 29 January 2026 after disabling Logic in June 2025 — two capabilities removed inside 18 months. Export gives you static HTML, CSS and JS, but CMS content, forms, search, ecommerce and memberships all stop working. Verdict: genuine AI depth, aimed at professionals who already own the tool. Not the shortest path for an owner who wants a finished site. 6. Hostinger Horizons — cheapest entry, one-way exit Hostinger's website builder page, leading with a $2.99/mo headline that requires a 48-month upfront commitment Blink Price: Premium $2.99/mo · Unlimited $3.99/mo · Cloud Startup $7.99/mo — all promotional. No free plan; 14-day trial, 30-day money-back guarantee. Best for: the lowest possible outlay, if you will prepay four years Horizons launched 20 February 2025 and reached general availability that March. It takes prompts in 80+ languages, accepts voice prompts and screenshot uploads, and auto-selects a stack — typically a Node.js backend with a React and Vite frontend. A custom domain is bundled free for the first year. Three things need translating before you buy. The headline is not a monthly price. Hostinger states: "All plans are paid upfront. The monthly rate reflects the total plan price divided by the number of months in your plan." That $2.99 is $143.52 charged upfront for 48 months , renewing at $10.99/mo — $131.88/yr thereafter. Unlimited renews at $203.88/yr, Cloud Startup at $311.88/yr. Prices exclude VAT, and the bundled .com renews at $19.99/yr. Two separate credit pools. "AI credits for website and app creation" — 5 on Premium, 15 on Unlimited — and separately "credits for AI agents": none on Premium, 500 on Unlimited, 1000 on Cloud Startup. Reverting your work with Undo does not refund the credits it consumed. Export is one-way. Horizons does export code, but Hostinger states "there is no way to import the edited version back to Horizons and continue with prompting." Hostinger's own pages also disagree on the format — the export article describes a Node.js/React/Vite project, the technical-specifications article describes a static website, and both were current on 18 August 2026. The exported bundle cannot be uploaded to Hostinger's own shared hosting as-is; it must be built to static files first, and running it live needs Business or Cloud hosting with Node.js apps, or a VPS. Horizons also has no FTP, SFTP or SSH, and no GitHub import. Verdict: the cheapest way to get something online, provided you understand the prepay and that the AI path does not run in reverse. 7. Squarespace — AI wrapped around the best templates in the category Squarespace's homepage, leading with template-driven design and a 14-day trial — there is no permanent free plan Blink Price: Basic $19/mo · Core $29/mo · Plus $49/mo · Advanced $99/mo, billed annually. No free plan — 14-day trial only. Best for: a portfolio, restaurant or boutique brand that wants to look excellent immediately and will not restructure Squarespace's design quality is real and it is the honest reason to pick it: roughly 200 designer templates, 4.6/5 across 3,415 Capterra reviews , and 99.96% uptime in Tooltester's own monitoring. Its AI investment is serious too — Blueprint AI, the Design Intelligence suite, a Squarespace GPT in the ChatGPT store, a partnership placing Squarespace inside Perplexity's Comet browser, and AI Visibility , launched 7 July 2026, which monitors where a business appears in AI-powered search and benchmarks competitors. The AI generates within the template system rather than replacing it, and that is the whole shape of the product. On 7.1 you cannot switch templates after launch. The export is a partial one-way WordPress-oriented XML file that omits style settings, custom CSS, store, portfolio, event and index pages, and every blog page beyond the first. And you cannot edit robots.txt or the sitemap — no page exclusion, no priority, no splitting by content type — which is a hard ceiling if organic search pays your bills. Tooltester measured its mobile page-speed score at 28.94, last among the twelve builders they tested. Prices also rose up to 26% on 17 July 2026, as PetaPixel reported . Verdict: if you want one beautiful site and will never restructure it, no one has a better catalogue to start from. Choose it knowing you are renting the design — the ceiling is how close your business sits to one of those 200 templates — and that you cannot tune the SEO plumbing. See Blink vs Squarespace . 8. WordPress Big Sky — free to try, narrow by design WordPress.com's homepage — the managed face of the open-source software that still runs roughly 41.9% of the web Blink Price: Personal $4/mo · Premium $8/mo · Business $25/mo · Commerce $45/mo, billed annually. Big Sky's first 30 prompts are free. Best for: someone already committed to WordPress who wants a faster start Big Sky is WordPress.com's chat-style AI builder, launched in early access April 2025 and now offered to anyone creating a new WordPress.com site. The first 30 prompts are free, though publishing requires a paid plan. WordPress 7.0, released 20 May 2026, added a Web Client AI API to core. The vendor is explicit about the boundary, and it is a real one: Big Sky does not support building ecommerce stores or intricate integrations . It is a fast start for a content site, not a general-purpose builder. The wider WordPress trade still applies underneath it. You inherit the plugin layer — Patchstack recorded 11,334 new ecosystem vulnerabilities in 2025, 91% of them in plugins — and on self-hosted, promotional hosting reprices 4–6× at renewal. What you get in exchange is the best ownership story in the category: GPLv2 software you can self-host, where no vendor can lock you out. Verdict: worth the 30 free prompts if you are staying on WordPress anyway. Not a reason to choose WordPress. What a credit actually buys The mechanic that decides your bill is whether credits refresh daily or only monthly. Framer, Webflow and Wix reset monthly, so one heavy week can end your month; Lovable and Blink both add daily credits, and on Blink's paid plans those carry no monthly cap. Every tool here meters AI usage and no two meter it the same way, so this is the table nobody publishes. Then hand over a site the client edits by describing changes — which is how the project ends instead of turning into support. Webflow is the alternative worth knowing if you already employ a specialist and sell design craft as the deliverable. You are a solo founder who needs the site and the product. Use Blink . The database, six sign-in providers, storage and deployment are included rather than assembled, and mobile output via React Native and Expo is a first-class target — which no other tool on this page offers. And the case we will hand over: if you want one flawless template for a portfolio or restaurant and you will genuinely never restructure it, Squarespace has the better catalogue to start from. Take it, and accept the SEO ceiling that comes with it. That is an answer to a different question. If yours was how to get a site built, hosted and ranking without assembling three vendors, the answer is Blink. Frequently asked questions Yes, and the meaningful difference is what happens after generation. Blink generates the site to your description and also ships what runs behind it — a per-project SQL database, six authentication providers, file storage, hosting on a custom domain with automatic SSL, and an SEO panel that scores the live site 0–100 and applies fixes. The site is finished and published rather than handed to you as a draft. Because most AI website builders generate into a template rather than designing from your brief. The layout, section order and spacing were fixed before you typed anything, so the AI's job is to pick the closest template and populate it — which is why the output is recognisable at a glance. Tools that generate the structure itself from a description do not share that ceiling. The test is to ask for a change the template cannot anticipate, such as moving testimonials above pricing: on a template-based builder that is a project, and on a brief-based one it is a sentence. It depends entirely on the controls the platform gives you, not on the AI. Squarespace is the weakest here — you cannot edit robots.txt or the sitemap, cannot exclude pages or set priority, and canonical and advanced schema control is limited.
